ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the closed loop L is drawn as an ellipse, and the arrow below the ellipse indicates the direction of integration along L. The current line I_1 passes through the inside of the ellipse on the left side, with the arrow upward; the current line I_2 passes through the inside of the ellipse in the middle, with the arrow downward; the current line I_3 is on the right side, located outside the ellipse L, with the arrow upward. Reasoning: By Ampere's circuital theorem, \(\oint_L \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{r}=\mu_0 I_{\text{enc}}\). According to the arrow direction of loop L, use the right-hand rule to determine the positive normal direction; under this convention, in the figure, the direction in which \(I_1\) passes through the enclosed surface is positive, the direction in which \(I_2\) passes through the enclosed surface is negative, while \(I_3\) is not enclosed by L and is not counted in the through current. Therefore the algebraic enclosed current is \(I_{\text{enc}}=I_1-I_2\). So \(\oint_L \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{r}=\mu_0(I_1-I_2)\).

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram: the path L encloses the first two current lines but not the third. Determine the positive normal from the arrow on L by the right-hand rule. With that convention, I1 crosses the surface in the positive direction and I2 crosses in the negative direction; I3 is not enclosed and contributes zero. Therefore the enclosed algebraic current is I1 - I2, giving ∮_L B·dr = μ0(I1 - I2).
